newsitem.title: UK: Minister proposes shake up of Britain's courts.
newsitem.headline: Minister proposes shake up of Britain's courts.

text.p: Home Secretary Michael Howard, keen to boost the reputation of his ruling Conservatives as the party of law and order, unveiled wide-ranging plans on Thursday to cut delays in bringing criminal cases to court.
But the 33 proposed changes were dismissed by the opposition Labour party Jack Straw, as "too little, too late".
Howard told parliament the proposals include cutting the age at which young people can be tried in adult courts to 17 from 18 and limiting the right of defendants to trial by jury.
"Justice delayed is justice denied," Howard said. "These proposals have the potential...to afford justice more speedily."
But Labour's home affairs spokesman, Jack Straw, said the proposals showed the "neglect and complacency" of the Conservative government, which has been in office for 18 years.

"To issue a document like this eight weeks before a general election is a doubtful way in which the Home Secretary can regain the initiative on law and order which the Conservative party has so comprehensively lost," Straw told parliament.
Labour, which has been dragged from the left to the centre by its leader Tony Blair and has successfully challenged the Conservatives on law and order issues, has a 20 point poll lead.

Commentators who saw Howard's announcement as window-dressing before an election which must be called by May pointed out that the government is seeking reaction to the proposals from people working in the criminal justice system.
This means they cannot be implemented before the election and will not form part of the ruling party's campaign pledges.
But the proposals could still prove controversial.

Howard has frequently clashed with judges, who have accused him of putting political considerations before justice, and the Law Society immediately criticised the proposal to curb rights to trial by jury as unjust and unnecessary.

"The citizen's right to trial by a jury of his or her peers must continue... The interests of bureaucracy in the criminal justice system should never come before the interests of justice," said the society, Britain's lawyers' association.
